To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
rye aleurones improve insulin economy compared with wheat aleurones and whole-wheat grain.
rye aleurones are a rich source of fermentable carbohydrates and that rye breads prepared from rye aleurons are able to improve insulin secretion in pigs fed a high-fibre diet.
breads prepared from wheat and rye aleurones are able to improve insulin secretion in comparison to breads prepared from WWG.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of breads made from WWG, WAF and RAF on net portal absorption and apparent insulin response.
the effects of whole-wheat grain, wheat and rye aleuronic fractions on the insulin response to breads in pigs.
the effects of whole-wheat grain, wheat aleurone and rye aleuron on insulin secretion and portal absorption of glucose, SCFA and lactic acid in pigs fed bread.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the fermentation-derived products in rye breads are linked to an improved insulin response in pigs.

bread made from whole grain, aleurone flour from wheat or rye and the corresponding white flour (WWG, WAF and RAF) were all able to reduce the postprandial insulin response, and the reduction was more pronounced when whole grain or aleurone flour was used compared to white flour.
the effects of bread on insulin economy are related to the content of DF and the composition of the DF.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
breads made from rye ingredients are better than wheat ingredients in terms of insulin economy.
rye breads, especially those containing aleurone fractions, have beneficial effects on insulin secretion and insulin sensitivity in humans.
breads prepared from WWG, WAF and RAF were similar in dietary DF content, but the DF was of different origin, and this resulted in different insulin responses.
The main takeaway from our work is that
rye aleuronal fibre has a beneficial effect on glucose homeostasis in pigs.
the fermentation products from rye aleurones may be beneficial in terms of insulin economy.
the fermentation products in the gastrointestinal tract of pigs fed RAF bread were linked to a low insulin response.
